data.title: The Clarity Act is DEAD
data.transcript_raw: The most heavily lobbied piece of legislation in crypto's history just went to the Senate floor and lost 49 to 50. But, the weird thing is the Senate didn't reject the Clarity Act. It actually refused to debate it at all because that vote wasn't about passing anything. It was a cloture vote on the motion to proceed, which is political language for are we allowed to start talking about this? So, 2 years of lobbying work and a crypto war chest that started the cycle at $193 million and the industry still couldn't buy permission to open the conversation. So, what actually killed [music] Clarity and what happens now? Well, to answer those questions, we'll look at why a technical market structure bill became a political issue, why the timing makes this final, and who ends up writing crypto's rulebook now that Congress has walked away from it. My name is Guy and this [music] is the Coin Bureau. So, what was actually on the table here? Well, Clarity was supposed to be the ultimate crypto rulebook. It drew a line between two agencies, the CFTC, which would take primary oversight of decentralized coins like Bitcoin, and the SEC, which would keep the ones still behaving like securities. It set a definitive test for when a token stops being a security, structured around whether insiders still have control over supply and governance. It gave exchanges a federal registration path and customer fund segregation rules written specifically so nobody could commingle client money the way FTX did. And it carved out protections for developers, node operators, and validators. It was also intended to sit on top of the Genius Act, the stablecoin law signed last year. So, stablecoins already have their statute and market structure was the missing half. And the house had done its part a long time ago, passing the bill 294 to 134 in July 2025 with 78 Democrats voting for it. That is about as bipartisan as crypto has ever been in Washington. So then, how does a bill with that much momentum die [clears throat] in the Senate? Well, because somewhere in the 14 months it spent stuck there, it became a partisan issue. Every month of delay attached another argument to it, and by September, none of those arguments were about crypto market structure. No, they were about one family's crypto portfolio. President Trump reported more than 1.4 billion dollars in crypto-related income for 2025, spread across World Liberty Financial, the USD 1 stablecoin, and the Trump meme coin launched days before his second inauguration. World Liberty is run with involvement from Don Jr. and Eric Trump, and it secured conditional approval from the OCC for a national trust bank charter. The widely held view of that was that Trump had become the first president to approve, operate, and regulate a bank connected to his own family. And that's the backdrop every Democrat was voting against. The sponsors knew this, and over last weekend, Senators Lummis, Boozman, and Scott released a 635-page substitute text with more than 100 Democrat requested changes, including a last-minute ethics package. That package barred the president, vice president, members of Congress, judges, and their spouses from issuing new digital assets while in office, forced divestment or blind trusts above a $15,000 interest, and even gave state attorneys general standing to sue. The White House had resisted that one for months. But the Democrats read that and said, "Nope." And their objections were quite specific. The ban only applied going forward, so it touched nothing already earned. Also, it covered issuing tokens, not stablecoin reserve interest or equity sales, which is where most of the money actually was. Enforcement depended on a Justice Department headed by Todd Blanche, Trump's former personal defense lawyer. And per the more detailed accounts, the whole thing was written to expire in January 2029 anyway. Senator Elizabeth Warren called it, quote, "a weak fig leaf that will do nothing to stop him from making his next $1.4 billion in crypto profits." Senator Lummis said the text was as good as it's going to get, and well, that was that. In the 2024 cycle, the crypto industry's main political spending network, Fairshake, raised over $260 million and spent $140 million across more than 70 congressional races, including around $40 million targeting a single Ohio senator. Coinbase put in $86 million cumulatively, Ripple $45 million. So, going into 2026, Fairshake carried a war chest of about $193 million, and by midyear filings had raised nearly $137 million more for the cycle. Public Citizen's tracking had crypto, AI, and online betting accounting for over $294 million of corporate election spending in the first 15 months of the cycle, with crypto the largest sector of the whole lot. And Fairshake backed candidates won 50 [laughter] of 54 contested primaries. So, the industry did everything it possibly could to push its interests. But apparently, it couldn't buy the remaining votes it needed. And that's because the obstacle was a live battle over conflict of interest involving a sitting president. And there's no campaign contribution that resolves that. Which brings us to the unfortunate reality that this probably spells the end of the Clarity Act, at least in its current form. The Senate never passed its own version of the bill, so there's nothing for lawmakers to merge with the version that already passed the House. And time is basically gone. The House has already left Washington to campaign, while the Senate is about to head into its own break before the midterms. Now, as you can see, crypto regulation can change direction sharply in just a matter of days, which makes these stories very easy to lose track of if you're not watching them closely. So, to make sure you don't miss the major developments that impact your portfolio, come and join us over on the Coin Bureau Telegram channel. That's where we share breaking news, on-chain alpha, and the market updates that matter the second they land. To get involved, just hit the link down in the description or scan the QR code on screen. Now, just because the Clarity Act didn't go as planned doesn't mean Washington forgets all about crypto. Back in March, the SEC and CFTC jointly said major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum should be treated as commodities rather than securities. They also put staking, mining, and certain airdrops outside securities treatment. Then, just last month, SEC Chair Paul Atkins proposed a much broader crypto rulebook, and the two agencies signed a memorandum of understanding agreeing to coordinate their approach. Over at the CFTC, Chairman Mike Selig directed staff to explore market structure rules using existing authority, in his words, to help the president deliver if Congress will not. So, crypto asked Congress for a law and ended up getting the regulators instead. But really, for the industry right now, that doesn't seem like much of a loss because both chairs are about as crypto-friendly as they've ever been. But there is something important worth mentioning here. Atkins built those rules explicitly as a bridge. He said the framework drew heavily on clarity and would give the agencies a head start implementing the market structure legislation he trusted would soon reach the president's desk. He said that before the 15th of September vote. The agencies never intended to be the permanent answer. But they have essentially become it by default. And even Selig has said that legislation is the most reliable approach because a law is considerably harder for a future administration to reverse. A proposed regulatory rule can be rescinded, challenged under the Administrative Procedure Act, or unwound by a future Congress through the Congressional Review Act. For a bit of context, Commissioner Hester Peirce, who led the crypto task force this whole framework grew out of, is expected to depart in November, which would leave the SEC with two sitting commissioners mid-rulemaking. And Selig has been operating as the only Senate-confirmed commissioner on a five-seat panel. And yet, while the industry never got its clarity, it keeps chugging along anyway. Stablecoins went from a supply of $124 billion at the end of 2023 to over $300 billion today. USDC circulation hit $75 billion, up 73% year-on-year. Circle, meanwhile, picked up a national trust bank charter from the OCC just this summer. And recently, 21 institutions, including Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, and Citigroup, announced a joint venture to issue their own compliant dollar stablecoin. Elsewhere, spot Bitcoin ETFs have taken in around $55 billion cumulatively, supporting $100 billion in assets. Tokenized real-world assets crossed $38 billion, and DTCC, which settles essentially every American stock trade, ran live tokenized Treasury and equity transactions in July with its full service scheduled for next month. So, plainly, none of that needed clarity. Although, in fairness, the rejection of the Clarity Act did have a price, and the market has been paying it. The whole market took a hit once it was confirmed that the cloture vote had failed. And as I make this video, Bitcoin is down 13% year-to-date, Ethereum down about 19%, and Coinbase's stock down nearly 24%, falling around 9% on the day of the vote itself. So, the market didn't like this rejection. The industry was heavily focused on this statute, treating it as some kind of finish line. But as I just mentioned, capital has been flowing into crypto even without a proper rulebook. Crypto will certainly get a comprehensive market structure bill eventually, and until then, the industry will just keep on growing as it has been without one. But what do you think? Was this crypto's biggest political defeat or is this the moment crypto realizes it never needed permission to thrive in the first place? Let us know your thoughts in the comments down below. And if you want to get the full breakdown of how the dollar itself is being rebuilt on crypto infrastructure while all this has been going on, then check out our video on that right over here. As always, thank you so much for watching, and I'll see you again very soon. This is Guy signing off.
